# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

   is why `--pr` is still required on an approval — a park nobody can act on is not
   a park). The standing status is also what stops the next scheduler run adopting
   the same issue again; clearing it is a person's decision, made after reading what
   the run said. Only an item filed under the older shadow model writes back to a
   different issue, and the command does that too.

   Only `task:status:needs-human-failure` (and a park whose kind cannot be decoded) holds the
   task's lane — while one is open the generator files no further occurrence of
   this task. The other three wait for their human while the schedule carries on,
   so leaving one open costs nobody but the person it names.

   The `claudinite-task-exec` record goes onto the item, in the same comment, and
   the command writes it — Actions logs expire and the item does not, so the item
   is where a record has to live. Nothing here is yours to print by hand.

7. **Capture this session before you end it.** Last step, after the item is
   converged, and run it whichever way step 6 went:

   ```bash
   CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE=<n> node <engine>/hooks/session-end-command.mjs
   ```

   That runner invokes whatever session-end steps this repo's declared packs
   contribute; it knows nothing about what any of them do, and a repo that
   contributes none does nothing. Nobody is sitting in front of this session, so it
   ends by having its container reclaimed — precisely the ending that fires no
   `SessionEnd` hook. Left to the hook, every unattended run would leave no record
   of itself anywhere: not of the skills it loaded, not of the checks that caught
   something, not of how the work actually went, and not of the record you just
   printed. `CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE` is what files those logs under the item that
   ran, rather than under nothing.

   It cannot fail your run — the item is already converged and this changes nothing
   on GitHub. If it reports an error, **say so plainly in your final message** and
   end anyway.

## The one standing bound

You execute **this one item and nothing else**. Never list other work items,
never sweep the queue, never act on a second issue in this session — however
obviously stuck another one looks. Recovery is code that runs elsewhere, and a
session that helps out is how one item becomes three duplicate PRs.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

# tidy-issues worker

The **acting** half of the repo tidy-up: triage the issues in scope, then record what you did. The run's
**Context section is binding scope** — it lists the issues to triage. Work only those; don't enumerate the
repo yourself. GitHub access is **MCP-only** (`mcp__github__*`).

This task writes **issues only** (its triage actions and its own tracker). It never opens, closes, merges,
or comments on a PR — that dimension belongs to `tidy-prs`, which is assess-only.

## 1. Triage each issue

For each issue in the Context list, run the [single-issue-triage](../../skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)
skill. The skill owns the action ladder and the safeguards: "implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual
ask is true of `main`'s content **now** — verified there and cited, never inferred — and when the check is
inconclusive it **comments, doesn't close** — and an issue whose verdict is the one the skill
already posted there returns `unchanged`, written to nowhere. Collect what each triage did.

## 2. Reconcile this task's tracker

**Only a run that changed something reaches the tracker.** What counts is a triage action actually taken —
an issue closed, a comment posted — or something this run leaves for a human. `left` and
`unchanged` are not actions. A run that worked its whole Context list and took no action has
**nothing to record**: leave the tracker exactly as found, no body rewrite and no comment, and
create none if it doesn't exist. The scan itself is not news.

One standing tracker issue per repo, titled exactly `Claudinite tracker: Tidy Issues` — found by that
**exact title, never a fuzzy match**; create it **already closed** when there is something to record and it
is absent — creation always lands an issue open and ignores a `state: closed` argument, so create it and
close it in a second call (never a fresh issue per run, never a bare number that can dangle). Each dimension
keeps its **own** tracker, so the two tasks never race to rewrite one body.

Touch it two ways on a run that has something to record:

- **Rewrite the issue body** to today's **dated** snapshot: the actions taken this run and anything left
  for a human. The body is the live picture — it replaces yesterday's, it doesn't accumulate.
- **Add a dated comment** with today's status, so the body's snapshots leave a per-run trail.

Keep both short. **Never open, close, or reopen the tracker** — its state carries no meaning (the body is
the live picture; the state is just however it was created).

## 3. Retire the legacy tracker (transitional, one line of work)

Repos tidied before the split carry a single combined tracker titled exactly `Claudinite tracker: Repo
Tidy`. If it exists and its body doesn't already say so, rewrite the body to one line pointing at the
per-dimension trackers (`Tidy Issues`, `Tidy PRs`) and stop there — nothing else to do on it, and never
open, close, or reopen it. Already pointing at them ⇒ skip. Absent ⇒ skip; never create it.

`model: sonnet` — the implemented-in-`main` call is judgment; the reconcile is mechanical aggregation.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/single-issue-triage

# Single-issue triage

Triage **one** open issue and take the **first** applicable action. This **acts** — but every action
defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

- **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (`completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it
  landed.
- **Conflicts with a current guideline** → label `needs-decision` + a comment naming the conflict.
- **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
- **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it.
- **Else** → leave it.

**Every checkbox in the issue body ticked** is the author's own claim that the work is done — the
strongest completion signal an issue can carry, and the one thing that puts an otherwise quiet issue
into the first rung. It is **a claim, not proof**: read it as a reason to run the implemented-in-`main`
check, never as the answer. Verified ⇒ close; not ⇒ comment naming what is still missing. A
partially-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage the issue as if it carried no boxes.
Where the ask has **no repo-side artifact** (a console setting, a routine only a human can touch), those
ticks by the issue's own author are the closing condition — say so and close.

**"Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content _now_** — confirm
it there and cite it. **Never** infer it from a linked PR merging or the issue merely looking done. If
you can't point to it, **comment, don't close.** Create a label if it's missing. Return `{ action,
note }` (action one of closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win/left/unchanged).

## Never re-post a verdict you already posted

A triage comment updates the issue, and an updated issue is the next window's touched-issue
trigger — so a comment that only restates the last one wakes this task again tomorrow, and again
the day after. The verdict is the news; re-deriving it is not.

Before writing anything, read the issue's comments and find the most recent one this task posted
— by its marker, or, on an issue triaged before the marker existed, by its wording. If the action
you are about to take is the one that comment already announced, **post nothing and change nothing**
(a label already on the issue included) and return `{ action: 'unchanged', note: '<action> since
<its date>' }`. Closing is never a repeat: it changes the issue's state and ends the sequence.

End every comment you post with this marker, alone on the last line:

```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```
Before delegating this large triage batch (60 issues), let me check the current git state to give agents accurate instructions for verifying "implemented in main."

content.text: Now I'll delegate the 61-issue triage across parallel agents, each following the exact `single-issue-triage` skill procedure. I'm splitting into 7 batches since the issues are independent of each other.

input.prompt:
You are performing GitHub issue triage on the repo `missingbulb/Claudinite`, as one batch of a larger repo-wide "tidy-issues" maintenance pass. This exact procedure ("single-issue-triage") is a checked-in, established skill in this repo used by many prior automated runs — you are fully authorized to close issues, add labels, and post comments per the ladder below. This is real production GitHub state; be precise and conservative per the safeguards below.

## Your batch — triage these issue numbers, each independently, one at a time
1509, 1482, 1501, 1485, 1478, 942, 1400, 1321, 1420

## Repo access
- Use ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__github__issue_read,mcp__github__issue_write,mcp__github__add_issue_comment" to load the GitHub tools (they are deferred until searched for).
- Use mcp__github__issue_read (method=get, get_comments, get_labels) to read each issue and its full comment history and labels.
- The local checkout at /home/user/Claudinite is a full git clone of this exact repo, checked out precisely at origin/main's current HEAD (commit a06898a). To verify "is X implemented in main" use Read/Grep/Glob/Bash directly against these local files — that IS main's current content, and is faster and more reliable than anything else. Do NOT modify, stage, or commit anything in this checkout — you are only reading it.
- Never touch any pull request. Never push branches or commits, never open a PR. This task writes GitHub issues only (comments, labels, close/open state).
- The labels `quick-win`, `needs-decision`, `blocked` already exist in this repo — just apply them via mcp__github__issue_write's `labels` field, don't try to create them.

## Procedure — run this exactly, per issue, independently

Triage **one** open issue and take the **first** applicable action. This **acts** — but every action
defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

- **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (`completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it
  landed.
- **Conflicts with a current guideline** → label `needs-decision` + a comment naming the conflict.
- **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
- **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it.
- **Else** → leave it.

**Every checkbox in the issue body ticked** is the author's own claim that the work is done — the
strongest completion signal an issue can carry, and the one thing that puts an otherwise quiet issue
into the first rung. It is **a claim, not proof**: read it as a reason to run the implemented-in-`main`
check, never as the answer. Verified ⇒ close; not ⇒ comment naming what is still missing. A
partially-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage the issue as if it carried no boxes.
Where the ask has **no repo-side artifact** (a console setting, a routine only a human can touch), those
ticks by the issue's own author are the closing condition — say so and close.

**"Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content _now_** — confirm
it there and cite the specific file/path/line. **Never** infer it from a linked PR merging or the issue merely
looking done or stale. If you can't point to it in the actual tree, **comment, don't close.**

### Never re-post a verdict you already posted

A triage comment updates the issue, and an updated issue is the next window's touched-issue
trigger — so a comment that only restates the last one wakes this task again tomorrow, and again
the day after. The verdict is the news; re-deriving it is not.

Before writing anything, read the issue's comments and find the most recent one this task posted
— by its marker `<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=... -->`, or, on an issue triaged before the
marker existed, by its wording. If the action you are about to take is the one that comment already
announced, **post nothing and change nothing** (a label already on the issue included) and treat the
outcome as `unchanged`. Closing is never a repeat: it changes the issue's state and ends the sequence.

End every comment you post with this marker, alone on the last line:
```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```
(where `<action>` is one of closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win)

If an issue is already closed when you look at it, do nothing to it — report it as `already-closed`.

## Output format

After triaging your whole batch, reply with ONLY these lines, one per issue, no other prose:
`#<n>: <action> — <one-line note>`
where action is one of: closed / needs-decision / blocked / quick-win / left / unchanged / already-closed

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/single-issue-triage

# Single-issue triage

Triage **one** open issue and take the **first** applicable action. This **acts** — but every action
defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

- **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (`completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it
  landed.
- **Conflicts with a current guideline** → label `needs-decision` + a comment naming the conflict.
- **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
- **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it.
- **Else** → leave it.

**Every checkbox in the issue body ticked** is the author's own claim that the work is done — the
strongest completion signal an issue can carry, and the one thing that puts an otherwise quiet issue
into the first rung. It is **a claim, not proof**: read it as a reason to run the implemented-in-`main`
check, never as the answer. Verified ⇒ close; not ⇒ comment naming what is still missing. A
partially-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage the issue as if it carried no boxes.
Where the ask has **no repo-side artifact** (a console setting, a routine only a human can touch), those
ticks by the issue's own author are the closing condition — say so and close.

**"Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content _now_** — confirm
it there and cite it. **Never** infer it from a linked PR merging or the issue merely looking done. If
you can't point to it, **comment, don't close.** Create a label if it's missing. Return `{ action,
note }` (action one of closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win/left/unchanged).

## Never re-post a verdict you already posted

A triage comment updates the issue, and an updated issue is the next window's touched-issue
trigger — so a comment that only restates the last one wakes this task again tomorrow, and again
the day after. The verdict is the news; re-deriving it is not.

Before writing anything, read the issue's comments and find the most recent one this task posted
— by its marker, or, on an issue triaged before the marker existed, by its wording. If the action
you are about to take is the one that comment already announced, **post nothing and change nothing**
(a label already on the issue included) and return `{ action: 'unchanged', note: '<action> since
<its date>' }`. Closing is never a repeat: it changes the issue's state and ends the sequence.

End every comment you post with this marker, alone on the last line:

```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```

{"number":1509,"title":"Re-open the withhold lane: a member's workflows are no longer static after adoption","body":"#1494 put `CLAUDINITE_VARS: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}` into the executor stub. Every member holds the reader as of `claudinite-tasks` 60831.3, and **not one holds the line** — because nothing delivers `.github/workflows/` any more.

## The premise that closed the lane is now false

The withhold-and-hand-to-the-agent path shipped in #649 and worked. `packs/claudinite-canary-repo/migrations/2026-08-14-workflow-probe-current/` is documented as *"the first record to materialize into `.github/workflows/`"*.

#1317 closed it on one stated ground, at `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/pack-update.mjs:238`:

> Nothing needs to: a member's workflows are static after adoption (#1317).

That was true when it was written. #1494 is the counterexample: a workflow change every member needs, with no route to them. The alternative on the table was 13 hand-opened PRs — which the canon's own standing decision rejects, because per-repo manual work reliably does not happen.

## What is actually still there

The lane was **emptied, not removed** — the `updates/*` convention, and exactly the reason it exists. All four seams survive:

| Seam | State |
|---|---|
| `registry.mjs` `WITHHOLD_CAPABLE_ENV` / `WORKFLOW_DEST` / skip-with-note | intact, live |
| `pack-update.mjs` `PENDING_DIR`, `stagedAt()` | emptied, addressable |
| `stagedFiles()` | live — the sweep uses it |
| `applyStageFor(specs, withheld)` | still takes and renders `withheld` |

What #1317 removed is four lines: `write` drops workflow paths (`:239`), `env: {}` makes the handshake permanently false (`:242`), the sweep deletes anything staged (`:266`), and `withheld` is hardcoded `[]` (`:311`).

**The credential question is settled.** The Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` can never push under `.github/workflows/` — that part of the doctrine is real, and GitHub rejects the whole ref, so writing one into a tree about to be pushed fails the entire converge. But the apply stage does not run on that token: it raises a work item for an agent session, and the Claude GitHub App carries `workflows: write`. That is what closes the loop, and it is why staging + apply-stage is the shape rather than a direct write.

## A false green found on the way

`applyMaterializations` guards workflow dests and reports `SKIPPED …(workflow file; this caller cannot deliver one)`. `applyRewrites` (`registry.mjs:140-155`) has no such guard:

```js
if (next !== text) { await write(file, next); done.push(file); }
```

`write` silently drops workflow paths, but `done.push(file)` runs regardless — so **a rewrite record targeting a workflow file reports success while writing nothing.** Nothing has hit it because no record rewrites a workflow yet; this change makes that the exact shape needed, so it must be fixed here. Two structurally-identical surfaces, one guarded.

## The work

1. `applyRewrites` gets the same guard and the same skip-with-note as `applyMaterializations`.
2. `pack-update.mjs` refills the four seams: stage workflow paths under `PENDING_DIR`, announce the handshake, collect the real `withheld`, and scope the sweep so it clears pre-existing staged files without deleting what this run just staged.
3. A `claudinite-tasks` migration record rewriting the executor to insert the `CLAUDINITE_VARS` line — a **rewrite**, not a materialize, so each member's own stamped `# claudinite:secrets` names survive. It carries `applyStage` so a session delivers the staged file.
4. Forced fleet delivery afterwards, since this is an engine-flow change.

{"number":1482,"title":"#1466's rule F fix shipped without a version bump, so no member can receive it","body":"PR #1466 widened janitor rule F (`orphanedParkItems`, `{ knownTaskIds }` → `{ tasks }`) but did **not** bump `packs/claudinite-tasks/pack.mjs`. The version stayed at `60830.5`, which #1464 had already published with the *old* rule.

A member re-vendors a pack directory only when canon's version exceeds the one it has installed. So every member that converged on `60830.5` took #1464's tree — old rule F — stamped it `60830.5`, and can never receive #1466's fix under that version.

## Verified in production

Four members, read straight off `main`:

| repo | `pack.mjs` version | `janitor-rules.mjs` signature |
|---|---|---|
| MissingBulbWebsite | `60830.5` | `orphanedParkItems(open = [], { knownTaskIds ...` |
| VascularColoring | `60830.5` | `orphanedParkItems(open = [], { knownTaskIds ...` |
| EdFringeNow | `60830.5` | `orphanedParkItems(open = [], { knownTaskIds ...` |
| ClaudiniteCanary | `60830.5` | `orphanedParkItems(open = [], { knownTaskIds ...` |

The stamp and the code beside it disagree. Canon at the same version carries `{ tasks }`.

## Observed effect

I woke `task-janitor` on all 14 members with a queue at 2026-08-30T22:00Z. Every run reported `claudinite-task-exec v1 claudinite-tasks/task-janitor [#N] success` with **no** `closed N superseded and M orphaned park(s)` health line, and closed nothing. The 17 retired-pack parks the widened rule targets are all still open — for example missingbulb/MissingBulbWebsite#170, #156 and #153, which sat in the queue while the rule ran against them.

Under the old rule this is correct behaviour: `grow_with_claudinite/rule-revalidation` canonicalizes to `claudinite-growth/rule-revalidation`, which the repo *does* carry, so `!knownTaskIds.has(...)` is false. The fix exists and is unreachable.

## Why this is not self-correcting

#1472 later bumped to `60830.6`, so a converge from here *will* deliver the fix — by luck, not by the mechanism. Had #1472 not landed, the fix would have sat in canon indefinitely with every member believing it was current. Nothing red would have said so: the members' stamps read exactly as they should.

## What is worth fixing beyond the bump

`ci-work-scope.mjs` already enforces `pack-version-bumped` — it blocked a change of mine on this exact pack earlier today. It did not fire for #1466, and understanding why is the durable part of this issue. The likely shape: the branch's version already differed from the last *released* version because #1464 had bumped it in the same window, so a comparison against a release baseline reads as "already bumped" while a comparison against `main` at merge time would not. Whatever the cause, a pack whose **content** changed under a version already published to members is the failure mode to catch, not merely a version equal to main's.

## Immediate remedy

Force `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/fleet-baseline` so every member converges to `60830.6`, then wake `task-janitor` fleet-wide. Until that happens, the janitor sweeps are no-ops for R4.

[{"id":5476860538,"body":"Comment class: other

Investigated as asked, starting from the reproduction: make the same change without a version bump and see whether the checks catch it. **They do. It is not an agent bug and not a bug in the check's logic — it is a gap in what the check is able to ask.** Handing this off with the mechanism established.

## The reproduction says the check works

Branched from `origin/main` (`e846728`), appended a comment line to `packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/janitor-rules.mjs`, bumped nothing, ran `check_the_work.mjs`:

```
[BLOCKING] pack-version-bumped  packs/claudinite-tasks/pack.mjs
  this change edits packs/claudinite-tasks/ but leaves its version at 60831.3
  Fix: raise `version` in packs/claudinite-tasks/pack.mjs to '60831.4' — the version
       is the whole delivery signal, so an edit that does not move it stays in the
       canon forever
```

So the naive form of this failure is caught, blocking, with the right file and the right fix. #1466 did not get through that way.

## What #1466 actually did

The squashed commit `7a73464a` edits five shipping files under `packs/claudinite-tasks/` with `version: '60830.5'` on both sides — apparently the exact thing the check forbids. But it also **adds a `VERSIONS.md` row for 60830.5**, which is not what an agent that simply forgot to bump would produce. That combination is the tell: the branch *did* bump, and the bump was erased by something after CI.

The timeline (UTC), from `packs/claudinite-tasks/pack.mjs`'s own history:

| time | commit | version |
|---|---|---|
| 15:28:54 | `316fc3cb` (#1454) | `60830.4` |
| **20:35:55** | `b7dcf020` (**#1464**) | **`60830.5`** |
| **20:49:36** | `7a73464a` (**#1466**) | **`60830.5`** |
| 21:44:38 | `e4c52479` (#1472) | `60830.6` |

#1466 branched while main was at `60830.4` and bumped to `60830.5` — correctly, and with its `VERSIONS.md` row. **#1464 then merged first, 14 minutes earlier, and took `60830.5` for itself.**

## Both halves reproduced

Reconstructed #1466's branch on the `60830.4` base (`git cherry-pick` of `7a73464a` onto `316fc3cb`, plus the bump to `60830.5` the squash later made invisible) and ran the work checks against that base:

```
$ node engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs --base 316fc3cb
EXIT=0
```

**The PR was legitimately green.** Then merged the colliding commit into it:

```
$ git merge --no-commit --no-ff b7dcf020
Auto-merging packs/claudinite-tasks/pack.mjs      ← no conflict
CONFLICT (content): .../test/queue/janitor-rules.test.mjs   ← a test file; ships to nobody
$ grep -o "version: '[^']*'" packs/claudinite-tasks/pack.mjs
version: '60830.5'
```

`pack.mjs` auto-merges silently, because both sides made the *identical* edit `60830.4` → `60830.5`. Git has nothing to flag. The one conflict is in a test file, which `compute-vendor-set` drops and which therefore cannot warn anybody about a delivery problem.

## Why the check cannot see this

`pack-version-bumped` is `scope: 'work'`, and its own header says why: *"the question is what THIS change did. The tree always contains a version number; only the diff says whether it moved with the content beside it."* Against its own merge-base, #1466 moved the version and recorded the row. Both questions it asks are answered correctly, and yes.

The question nobody asks is a different one, and it is not a work-scope question at all:

> **is the version this change lands on already published on `main` under different content?**

That is a *collision* between two branches, and it is invisible from inside either one. Two PRs racing to bump the same pack both pass, both merge cleanly, and the second one's content ships under a number the fleet already has — so `planPackUpdates` sees `installed >= canon` and never re-fetches. That is #939's failure mode exactly, arriving through a door the check was not built to watch.

**Cost here:** #1466's rule F widening reached no member. The next night's janitor swept with the old `{ knownTaskIds }` code across the whole fleet and closed nothing, which is what this issue was opened on.

## Notes for whoever picks this up

- The 21-hour window `60830.1` → `60831.3` carried **twelve** `claudinite-tasks` versions. At that merge rate the collision window is not an edge case; it is the normal condition, and the same race is available to every pack.
- Recording the row does not protect you — #1466 has a correct `VERSIONS.md` row for `60830.5`, and it is now the *second* row that would claim that number if #1464 had written one too. `versionRecorded` only asks whether a row exists, never whether the version is uniquely claimed.
- Worth checking whether any other pair in that window collided the same way; I only traced `claudinite-tasks`.
- Anything that fixes this has to run where both branches are visible — merge-queue ordering, a world-scope uniqueness assertion over `VERSIONS.md`, or making the bump non-literal so two branches cannot write the same bytes. Choosing between those is the design call, and I have deliberately not made it.

# Single-issue triage

Triage **one** open issue and take the **first** applicable action. This **acts** — but every action
defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

- **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (`completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it
  landed.
- **Conflicts with a current guideline** → label `needs-decision` + a comment naming the conflict.
- **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
- **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it.
- **Else** → leave it.

**Every checkbox in the issue body ticked** is the author's own claim that the work is done — the
strongest completion signal an issue can carry, and the one thing that puts an otherwise quiet issue
into the first rung. It is **a claim, not proof**: read it as a reason to run the implemented-in-`main`
check, never as the answer. Verified ⇒ close; not ⇒ comment naming what is still missing. A
partially-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage the issue as if it carried no boxes.
Where the ask has **no repo-side artifact** (a console setting, a routine only a human can touch), those
ticks by the issue's own author are the closing condition — say so and close.

**"Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content _now_** — confirm
it there and cite it. **Never** infer it from a linked PR merging or the issue merely looking done. If
you can't point to it, **comment, don't close.** Create a label if it's missing. Return `{ action,
note }` (action one of closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win/left/unchanged).

## Never re-post a verdict you already posted

A triage comment updates the issue, and an updated issue is the next window's touched-issue
trigger — so a comment that only restates the last one wakes this task again tomorrow, and again
the day after. The verdict is the news; re-deriving it is not.

Before writing anything, read the issue's comments and find the most recent one this task posted
— by its marker, or, on an issue triaged before the marker existed, by its wording. If the action
you are about to take is the one that comment already announced, **post nothing and change nothing**
(a label already on the issue included) and return `{ action: 'unchanged', note: '<action> since
<its date>' }`. Closing is never a repeat: it changes the issue's state and ends the sequence.

End every comment you post with this marker, alone on the last line:

```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```

{"number":1485,"title":"task-declaration-shape passes an unresolvable `automerge` policy, and the task then silently stops being scheduled","body":"`task-declaration-shape` is the blocking world rule that judges a task declaration's shape, and it validates the **value** of every enum field it covers — `frequency` and `agent_model` via `enumField`, `expected_outcome` against `OUTCOMES`. For `automerge` alone it tests only presence:

```js
// packs/claudinite-tasks/worldRules/task-declaration-shape.mjs:66
const hasMayAutomerge = /\bautomerge:\s*/.test(stripComments(text));
```

`hasMayAutomerge` is then used only to pair the field with the ceiling (`pr` without it, `none` with it). Nothing anywhere in the check asks whether the policy *resolves*. A declaration carrying a typo'd rule name, a retired term, or an `under:` scope the member's mount does not yet understand passes the check green.

## The failure that follows is silent, and it is not a parked PR

`discover.mjs` validates for real — `validateTaskDeclaration`, which does call `normalizePolicy` — and drops the task on any problem:

```js
// packs/claudinite-tasks/discover.mjs:67
const problems = validateTaskDeclaration(decl);
if (problems.length) {
  errors.push({ … });
  continue;          // ← the task never reaches `tasks`
}
```

Both consumers render those errors as a bare log line and nothing else — `scheduler-run.mjs:611` and `executor.mjs:630` are each `for (const e of errors) console.log(\`! ${e.what}\`)`. No finding, no work item, no non-zero exit. No world rule reads `discoverTasks()`' errors at all.

So the end state for one bad policy term is: **the task stops running entirely**, with green CI, a green scheduler run, and a single `!` line buried in an Actions log. A task that has quietly left the schedule is indistinguishable from one whose precondition keeps declining.

## Demonstrated

Against `missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite` at `claudinite-tasks` 60830.9, adding one task declaring `automerge: ['under:site/data && typo-not-a-rule-name!!']`:

```
probe task discovered? false
errors: …/task.mjs is not a valid task declaration: "automerge" is not a legal policy:
        "under:site/data && typo-not-a-rule-name!!" is not a policy term …

$ node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs
0 blocking, 1 advisory (world scope: all vs origin/main)
```

This was a live near-miss, not a hypothetical. ClaudiniteWebsite#375 landed `automerge: [\`under:${PROMOTED_DIR}\`]` while that member's mount still predated #1474 — `validateTaskDeclaration` returned a problem against the mount as it stood, so the weekly `site-stats` recount would have dropped out of discovery, while `check_the_world.mjs` reported 0 blocking on the branch and in CI. It came right only because the member's mount converged to 60830.9 a few hours later. A member on a slower converge, or a term that never becomes valid, gets no such rescue.

## Two ways to close it, and why I'd pick the second

**Resolve the policy inside `task-declaration-shape`.** Natural, but it fights the check's nature: it is a text scan, deliberately, so it never executes member code. Policies are not reliably literal — canon's own flagship example is now

```js
// packs/product-wiki/tasks/wiki-growth/task.mjs:36
automerge: [`under:${WIKI_ROOT} && doc-changes`],
```

a template literal over a module const, and ClaudiniteWebsite's `site-stats` has the same shape. A static extractor would have to skip exactly the computed cases most likely to drift, so it would pass the very declarations worth catching.

**Surface `discoverTasks()`' errors as findings.** That path already validates with full fidelity — it imports the module, so template literals and consts are resolved — and today its output is thrown away in a log line. One world rule that runs discovery and reports each error turns every class of invalid declaration, `automerge` included, into a blocking finding at author time, and needs no new validation logic. It also closes the same hole for the other fields, since any `validateTaskDeclaration` problem currently disappears the same way.

{"number":1478,"title":"Re-shelve claudinite-tasks by stage: src/ for the code, queue/ frozen as workflow ABI","body":"`packs/claudinite-tasks/` carries ~24 modules at its root. That is sediment, not design: `git log --follow` on any of them shows one event — `a248483` (#1326) copied the whole flat `engine/scheduler/` directory in with `C100`. The pack root *is* the old flat scheduler dir, and `queue/` is the one sub-system that had already been carved out inside it before the move.

## The stages are already separable

An import graph over the pack (tests excluded) collapses to five stages with **exactly one** backward edge:

| Stage | Cross-stage edges |
|---|---|
| schedule — `scheduler-run`, `readiness`, `schedule-board`, `create-work-item`, `tick`, `drain-dispatch` | ⚠️ one: `queue/scheduler-run.mjs:32` imports `pickOrder` from `queue/executor.mjs` |
| execute-code — `code-work`, `code-work-run`, `prework-run`, `secrets-bag` | none |
| execute-agent — `resolve-dispatch`, `validate-dispatch`, `invoke`, `executor-continuation` | none |
| finalize — `converge-item`, `verify-outcome`, `record-exec`, `land-pr`, `deliver-generated` | none (invoked as CLI from prose, never imported by the executor) |
| recover — `janitor-rules`, `workflow-failure`, `task-janitor` | none |

That edge is placement, not coupling. `queue/executor.mjs` (672 lines) hosts two functions that are not executor mechanics: `pickOrder` (ordering policy over the queue, called by the scheduler run) and `evaluatePrecondition` (the contract's evaluator, published through `shared-code/task-contract.mjs` and re-run by both sides). Extract those two and the DAG is strictly one-directional — at which point the `barriers` pack can enforce it pointed inward, with no bespoke check.

The kernel is small and falls out of fan-in: `queue/work-item.mjs` (14 importers), `merge-policy.mjs` (6), `calendar.mjs` / `task-contract.mjs` / `queue/anchors.mjs` (5 each), `run-record.mjs` (4), `queue/leases.mjs` (3).

## What cannot move

Two of these cannot be repaired by a converge, and they shape the whole layout:

1. **Workflow `run:` targets** — stamped into every member's `.github/workflows/` at adoption, the one directory a converge may never push to. Five frozen paths: `queue/scheduler-run.mjs`, `queue/drain-dispatch.mjs`, `queue/workflow-failure.mjs`, `queue/executor.mjs`, `queue/executor-continuation.mjs`. Moving one costs a human-merged PR per member.
2. **`executor.md` and `queue/instructions.md`** — CCR routine endpoints, a per-repo console setting (`adopt-pack` §4b). Moving one needs every member re-pointed by hand.
3. Engine-mandated names: `pack.mjs`, `worldRules/`, `workRules/`, `tasks/`, `skills/`, `migrations/` and the metadata files.

So `queue/` survives as exactly **five one-line re-export shims plus `instructions.md`**, with a header saying it is workflow ABI and may never hold logic again. Everything else internal goes under `src/`.

## `shared-code/` → `src/contract/`, with shims

The barrier's allow list names `packs/claudinite-tasks/shared-code` as the one path another pack may import (`.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/declared-checks.json`). The nine modules there are all `export *` — 52 lines total — so they curate nothing today; their whole value is being a stable address. `contract` names that better, and absorbs the existing `task-contract` sense rather than colliding with it: what a task must declare, and what another pack may import.

**It needs shims.** `planPackUpdates` (`packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/pack-update.mjs:76`) marks a pack `blocked` when its `minEngineVersion` exceeds the member's engine — **that pack alone is held back while its siblings land**. So a member can hold a new `claudinite-dashboard` beside a blocked `claudinite-tasks`; if the dashboard imports `src/contract/…` and the mount carries only `shared-code/`, that pack fails to load, the mount fails its self-test, the converge refuses to land at all, and the member cannot receive the version that would fix it. That is the #1004 class exactly. So: move the modules, leave `shared-code/*` re-exporting, retire them on a stamp-confirmable precondition — "no member's `packVersions['claudinite-tasks']` predates the rename" — never a date.

Reference inventory: 15 non-test import sites across 5 consumer packs (dashboard ×5, fleet-sheepdog, basics, growth, lifecycle), 17 in tests, 13 prose/config mentions, the barrier's allow-list string (which must name both paths during the window), and one cross-pack path reference in `claudinite-dashboard/test/pack.test.mjs` reading `claudinite-tasks/stubs/…`.

## Target layout

```
packs/claudinite-tasks/
  pack.mjs  README.md  VERSIONS.md  badge.svg
  executor.md                          ← frozen (console routine)
  worldRules/  workRules/  tasks/  migrations/     ← engine-mandated

  queue/                               ← FROZEN WORKFLOW ABI, nothing else ever
    scheduler-run.mjs  drain-dispatch.mjs  workflow-failure.mjs
    executor.mjs  executor-continuation.mjs        (5 one-line re-exports)
    instructions.md                    ← frozen (console routine)

  src/
    contract/    work-items  anchors  task-contract  merge-policy  signals
                 github  delivery  usage-format  wake          (barrier-allowed)
    model/       work-item  leases  calendar  anchors  task-contract
                 precondition ←extracted  merge-policy  model-map  run-record
                 built-in-tasks  discover  dispatch
    gh/          read  write  tracker  read-items
    signals/     collectors + for-task
    schedule/    run  readiness  schedule-board  create-work-item  tick
                 drain-dispatch  pick-order ←extracted
    execute/     loop  apply-status  heartbeat  suspend
      code/      code-work  run  prework-run  secrets-bag
      agent/     resolve-dispatch  validate-dispatch  invoke  continuation
      built-in/implement-request/   (NOT tasks/ — engine-owned, registered separately)
    finalize/    converge-item  verify-outcome  record-exec  land-pr
                 deliver-generated  narrow-diff  deliver-pr.md
    recover/     janitor-rules  workflow-failure
    adopt/       converge-workflows  hash-minute  stubs/

  shared-code/   ← 9 re-export shims → src/contract/, retired on the stamp
  test/          mirrors src/
```

**The invariant:** `src/model/` and `src/gh/` import nothing from a stage; stages import only downward; no stage imports another stage; `src/contract/` only re-exports.

## Also in scope

- `run.mjs` and `slots.mjs` at the pack root are shims for the retired slot scheduler. Nothing in the tree imports either, and `engine-pack-lane-shims.test.mjs` guards `engine/**` paths, not these — confirm against fielded history, then delete rather than relocate.
- `README.md` claims `engine/scheduler/*` still exists as shims. It does not; `engine/` has had no `scheduler` directory since #1326.

{"number":942,"title":"Dashboard sign-in: make deploying the code-exchange endpoint a task, not a paste","body":"The dashboard's sign-in path is built and tested (#935), but it stays dormant until the code→token endpoint is live somewhere. Today that step is "paste `oauth-exchange.mjs` into a Cloudflare Worker and set three environment variables by hand", which is the kind of step that does not happen — so every deployment falls back to the token-paste box.

This issue is the **canon-side work**: give the pack a deploy script and a task that put the endpoint live and prove it answers. Actually registering the App and running it against a real account is missingbulb/Shepherd#352.

## Why the endpoint has to exist at all

A static page cannot reuse a visitor's github.com login: session cookies are not sent to `api.github.com`, and the API refuses cookie auth cross-origin. So "no typing" has to mean an OAuth sign-in. The `code` → token exchange needs the app's **client secret** and targets an endpoint that sends **no CORS headers**, so it cannot happen in the browser — it needs one small hosted function.

## Its lifecycle, since this was the question that opened the issue

It is **called once per sign-in**, not once ever — the page keeps the token in `sessionStorage` and deliberately lets it die with the tab, so every new tab and every viewer is a fresh `code` and a fresh call. It is also a **standing prerequisite of the button**, not of the dashboard: `isOAuthConfigured` requires both `clientId` and `exchangeUrl`, so with the endpoint gone the page renders no Sign in button and quietly reverts to the token box. It never proxies repo data and stores nothing.

## Scope

- [ ] A deploy script in the pack that uploads the endpoint with its bindings and routes it.
- [ ] A `frequency: 'manual'`, `agent_model: 'none'` task wrapping it — the endpoint changes when its source, its client secret or its allowed origins change, and none of those is a cadence.
- [ ] It must **verify the deployed URL**, not trust the upload's own 200: a stranger's origin refused, an allowed origin with no code rejected. Nothing else gives those two answers.
- [ ] Its public half (`clientId`, the allowed origins) reads from the member's own declaration — the same file the site build reads — so the button and the endpoint it calls cannot be configured against different apps.
- [ ] Name the secrets it needs and let the queue park on a missing one rather than guessing.

Setting `exchangeUrl` stays out of scope: the endpoint is live the moment it deploys, but the button appears only once the member's declaration names the URL, and that is an edit to the member's own file. The run reports the exact value.

## Done when

You are performing GitHub issue triage on the repo `missingbulb/Claudinite`, as one batch of a larger repo-wide "tidy-issues" maintenance pass. This exact procedure ("single-issue-triage") is a checked-in, established skill in this repo used by many prior automated runs — you are fully authorized to close issues, add labels, and post comments per the ladder below. This is real production GitHub state; be precise and conservative per the safeguards below.

## Your batch — triage these issue numbers, each independently, one at a time
1332, 1331, 1214, 1313, 1322, 1323, 1347, 170, 1341

## Repo access
- Use ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__github__issue_read,mcp__github__issue_write,mcp__github__add_issue_comment" to load the GitHub tools (they are deferred until searched for).
- Use mcp__github__issue_read (method=get, get_comments, get_labels) to read each issue and its full comment history and labels.
- The local checkout at /home/user/Claudinite is a full git clone of this exact repo, checked out precisely at origin/main's current HEAD (commit a06898a). To verify "is X implemented in main" use Read/Grep/Glob/Bash directly against these local files — that IS main's current content, and is faster and more reliable than anything else. Do NOT modify, stage, or commit anything in this checkout — you are only reading it.
- Never touch any pull request. Never push branches or commits, never open a PR. This task writes GitHub issues only (comments, labels, close/open state).
- The labels `quick-win`, `needs-decision`, `blocked` already exist in this repo — just apply them via mcp__github__issue_write's `labels` field, don't try to create them.

## Procedure — run this exactly, per issue, independently

Triage **one** open issue and take the **first** applicable action. This **acts** — but every action
defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

- **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (`completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it
  landed.
- **Conflicts with a current guideline** → label `needs-decision` + a comment naming the conflict.
- **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
- **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it.
- **Else** → leave it.

**Every checkbox in the issue body ticked** is the author's own claim that the work is done — the
strongest completion signal an issue can carry, and the one thing that puts an otherwise quiet issue
into the first rung. It is **a claim, not proof**: read it as a reason to run the implemented-in-`main`
check, never as the answer. Verified ⇒ close; not ⇒ comment naming what is still missing. A
partially-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage the issue as if it carried no boxes.
Where the ask has **no repo-side artifact** (a console setting, a routine only a human can touch), those
ticks by the issue's own author are the closing condition — say so and close.

**"Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content _now_** — confirm
it there and cite the specific file/path/line. **Never** infer it from a linked PR merging or the issue merely
looking done or stale. If you can't point to it in the actual tree, **comment, don't close.**

### Never re-post a verdict you already posted

A triage comment updates the issue, and an updated issue is the next window's touched-issue
trigger — so a comment that only restates the last one wakes this task again tomorrow, and again
the day after. The verdict is the news; re-deriving it is not.

Before writing anything, read the issue's comments and find the most recent one this task posted
— by its marker `<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=... -->`, or, on an issue triaged before the
marker existed, by its wording. If the action you are about to take is the one that comment already
announced, **post nothing and change nothing** (a label already on the issue included) and treat the
outcome as `unchanged`. Closing is never a repeat: it changes the issue's state and ends the sequence.

End every comment you post with this marker, alone on the last line:
```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```
(where `<action>` is one of closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win)

If an issue is already closed when you look at it, do nothing to it — report it as `already-closed`.

## Output format

After triaging your whole batch, reply with ONLY these lines, one per issue, no other prose:
`#<n>: <action> — <one-line note>`
where action is one of: closed / needs-decision / blocked / quick-win / left / unchanged / already-closed
